paras: The lynching of Graves was the hanging of a 16-year-old Black boy by a mob near Brownstown, Sevier County, Arkansas, late on the night of Friday, August 24, 1888. He had been accused of assaulting the five-year-old daughter of a white farmer, and the mob took him from the officers who held him. A brief dispatch from Little Rock carried the news to papers across the country, and later summaries gave a different charge.

According to the Little Rock dispatch of August 27, on the previous Thursday Graves, described as a 'negro boy, sixteen years old,' 'outraged' the five-year-old daughter of Joseph A. Tally, a white farmer living near Brownstown. The Washington Critic printed the charge as 'assaulted', and the dispatch reported the girl's condition as 'deemed critical.'

Graves was in the hands of officers by the next night. Late Friday night a mob 'forcibly took Graves from the officers and hanged him to a limb of a neighboring tree.' A rewritten version in a Dakota weekly said the mob acted 'shortly after learning of the deed.' None of the reports names the officers or any member of the mob, or gives the mob's size.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and no later word on the girl's condition was found.

The dispatch ran on August 28 in the Memphis Appeal under 'An Arkansas Lynching', in the Savannah Morning News as 'A Young Ravisher Lynched', in the New York Sun as 'A Negro Boy Lynched' and in the Omaha Daily Bee as 'A Negro Brute Lynched.' The Washington Critic and the Indianapolis Journal folded it into columns of short news items, and the Indianapolis paper misplaced Sevier County in Tennessee. Every version stated the accusation as fact and named the girl's father, while the mob stayed anonymous.

Weekly papers then shrank the story to a single line in their news summaries, as the Stanford, Kentucky, Interior Journal did on August 31 and the Peninsula Enterprise of Accomac, Virginia, did on September 1, which spelled the farmer's name 'Tolly.' The Hillsboro, Ohio, News-Herald reprinted the full dispatch as late as September 6, and the Wessington Springs Herald in Dakota printed a reworded version on September 7.

A separate summary item, first seen in the Narragansett Herald on September 1, said a mob took 'John Graves, a sixteen-year-old colored boy from jail at Brownstown, Ark., and lynched him for an unprovoked murder he had committed.' The same item ran in the West Virginia Argus on September 6 and the Abbeville Press and Banner on September 12. This version names no murder victim and differs from the dated Little Rock dispatch on the charge and on whether Graves was held by officers or in jail; the earlier dispatch is the more detailed source.

reader.title: Lynching of Graves
bases: A mob took Graves, a Black boy, from officers holding him and hanged him from a tree after he was accused of a crime (A3, A1, A8).

Every report says a mob took Graves from officers (or from jail) and hanged him, with no lawful process (A3, A1, A8). The mob acted on an accusation of assault on a child, or in one version of murder, which is a pretext of punishing a crime (A3, A8).

Every report traces to one Little Rock dispatch of Aug. 27 (A3, A1, A2) or to a shortened rewrite of it (A8, A10, A13); no local Arkansas report or independent second account was found, though all copies agree that a mob hanged Graves.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire report
accounts.gist: On Thursday Graves, a 16-year-old Black boy, 'outraged' Joseph A. Tally's five-year-old daughter; late Friday night a mob took him from the officers and hanged him to a tree limb. The girl's condition was critical.

accounts.label: Weekly news-summary brief
accounts.gist: A mob took John Graves, a 16-year-old 'colored boy', from jail at Brownstown, Ark., and lynched him 'for an unprovoked murder he had committed'.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Little Rock dispatch almost word for word, stating the accusation as fact and naming the girl's father but not the mob.
Savannah's 'A Young Ravisher Lynched' and Omaha's 'A Negro Brute Lynched' headlines labeled the boy by the charge against him.
Weekly news summaries gave the lynching one line among accidents and crimes.

versions.value: assault ('outraged'/'assaulted') on the five-year-old daughter of Joseph A. Tally

conflicts.note: The assault version is the dated Little Rock dispatch that ran first; the murder version appears only in a later undated summary brief that names no victim of the supposed murder, and looks like a garbled rewrite.
Both versions have him in custody; the first dispatch says officers, the later brief says jail.
Only the summary brief gives a first name.
The Indianapolis Journal's 'Tennessee' contradicts its own wire text's Little Rock origin as printed elsewhere; every other copy says Arkansas.
The dispatch says Tally lived near Brownstown and the hanging was at 'a neighboring tree'; the briefs shorten this to 'at Brownstown'.

record_check.dossier: Graves; one later brief gives 'John Graves'.

record_check.dossier: Supported by the wire dispatch; one later brief says instead 'an unprovoked murder', which should be noted as a conflict.
Near Brownstown (the dispatch places the Tally farm near the town and the hanging at a neighboring tree).
Supported: hanged late Friday night before the Monday, Aug. 27 dispatch.
Conflicts exist over the charge (assault vs. murder), custody (officers vs. jail), and state (one copy says Tennessee).

info: Accused of the assault on Thursday (Aug. 23, 1888) and hanged late Friday night (Aug. 24, 1888), going by the Monday, Aug. 27 Little Rock dateline.
Near Brownstown (spelled 'Brounston' and 'Browstown' in some copies); one brief says at Brownstown, another says from the jail at Brownstown.
Graves, a 'negro boy' or 'colored boy', 16 years old; one brief names him John Graves.
Accused of having 'outraged' (or 'assaulted') the five-year-old daughter of Joseph A. Tally, a white farmer living near Brownstown; the girl's condition was reported critical.
'a mob'; no members named and no race stated.
